findings.text: The test claims that "`\#"` does not end `#"…"#`", but `x\#"y` contains no `"#` at all. Without the escape handling, the closer would still be the later `z"#`, and the line would count the same. Neither assertion on lines 236–237 can tell escape handling apart from no handling (on 237, both readings leave line 1 as code and line 2 as a comment). The `\#` rule is the only thing that makes a raw string go on past a `"#` / `"""#`, and it is effectively untested. A test that would catch it: `#"""`, `\#"""#`, `// x`, `"""#`. With escape handling the `// x` line is code; without it, that line becomes a comment.

In the multi-line raw string, the line `/* a "" """ \#"""` holds no `"""#` closer whether or not `\#` is skipped, because `"""` sits at the end of the line with no `#` after it. So it does not exercise the `\#` escape inside `#"""…"""#`, which its placement suggests it does.

The test is meant to show that `bar"x"` is an identifier followed by a string, not the raw string `r"x"`. But `"x"` closes at the same `"` whether it is read as a raw or an escaped string, so the assertion passes even with no identifier check. The string needs to contain a backslash before a quote to tell the two apart, e.g. `bar"\"/*"` followed by a `// d` line.

Of the character literals in this test, only `'"'` (line 201) affects the count. In Rust a `'` that is not taken as a literal opens nothing, so `'\''`, `'\\'`, `'\u{1F600}'` and `'😀'` (lines 202–205) count the same even if `RUST_CHAR` rejects them. The escape forms the goal lists are therefore not verified. Only a literal holding a quote shows a difference, e.g. `'\"'` (an escaped double quote) followed on later lines by a comment; it is not tested.

blind.summary: I traced every case the goal lists through `readLine`, and the implementation handles all of them correctly. That covers Rust nested comments (including the overlapping `/*/` and `*/*` forms, matched against rustc's lexer), raw and byte strings with any number of `#`, the identifier check before `r`/`b`, and character literals versus lifetimes and labels. For Swift it covers nested comments, `"…"`, `"""…"""`, `#"…"#` and `#"""…"""#` with the `\#…` escape rule, and `#if`/`#selector`. For Lua it covers `--[==[ ]==]` comments, `[==[ ]==]` strings, the `--[`, `--[=x` and `---[[` line comments, and quoted strings. Other languages are unaffected, because every new code path is gated on the new syntax flags. I found no blocker or major bug. The defects left are tests that would pass even with the behaviour they name broken. Nothing was run: the review was read-only, and the test results come from working them through by hand.
